opening_arguments.for:
Honourable judges, respected opponents, and colleagues:

I stand for the proposition that **Islam promotes peace**. Not merely peace as the absence of war, but peace as a moral order: peace with God, peace within the self, peace in society, and peace among nations.

The very word **Islam** is connected to the Arabic root *s-l-m*, associated with peace, safety, and wholeness. The everyday greeting of Muslims is **“as-salāmu ʿalaykum” — “peace be upon you.”** This is not incidental; it reflects a central ethical vision.

Islam’s core scripture repeatedly establishes peace, justice, mercy, and restraint as foundational values. The Qur’an declares:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

This is a direct rejection of forced faith. If Islam were inherently coercive or violent, this principle would make no sense.

The Qur’an also teaches the sanctity of human life:

> “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely.”  
> **Qur’an 5:32**

That is one of the strongest possible statements of the value of human life.

Islam also commands justice even toward opponents:

> “Do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> **Qur’an 5:8**

This is crucial. Islam does not say, “Be peaceful only with those who agree with you.” It says justice must apply even when emotions, conflict, and hostility are present.

When dealing with people of other communities, the Qur’an states:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion or expelled you from your homes. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.”  
> **Qur’an 60:8**

So peaceful coexistence is not a modern addition to Islam; it is embedded in the Qur’an itself.

Now, critics may point to verses about fighting. But responsible debate requires context. Islam does not deny that armed conflict may occur; almost every moral and legal tradition recognizes self-defence. But the Qur’an strictly limits warfare:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> **Qur’an 2:190**

And it further commands:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> **Qur’an 8:61**

This is not a doctrine of aggression. It is a doctrine of restraint: fight only those who fight you, do not transgress, and accept peace when peace is offered.

The Prophet Muhammad’s teachings reinforce this. He said:

> “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 10; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 40**

This definition is powerful: a true Muslim is not measured by slogans, but by whether others are safe from his harm.

He also said:

> “None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 13; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 45**

And in another narration:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3166**

That last teaching is especially relevant because it protects non-Muslims living under Muslim protection or treaty. It shows that violating the life and safety of peaceful non-Muslims is not only illegal but spiritually condemned.

Islam’s ethical vision is also summarized in this Qur’anic command:

> “Indeed, God commands justice, excellence, and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression.”  
> **Qur’an 16:90**

Justice, excellence, charity, and opposition to oppression: these are not marginal values in Islam; they are central.

Therefore, the proposition that “Islam promotes peace” is supported by Islam’s scripture, its prophetic teachings, and its legal-ethical principles. Like all major traditions, Islam has been misused by individuals and political powers. But the misuse of a religion does not define its essence. We do not judge democracy by every war fought by democratic states; we do not judge Christianity by the Crusades; and we should not judge Islam by extremists who violate its own teachings.

Islam promotes peace through the sanctity of life, freedom of conscience, justice toward enemies, kindness toward peaceful others, strict limits on warfare, and a moral ideal in which people are safe from harm.

For these reasons, I proudly affirm the proposition: **Islam promotes peace.**
opening_arguments.against:
Chair, judges, and audience—

I oppose the proposition **not because Muslims as people are inherently violent**—they are not, and millions of Muslims live peacefully—but because the proposition says something much stronger: that **Islam, as a religious system of scripture, law, and historical practice, promotes peace**. That claim is too broad and cannot survive scrutiny.

Islam contains peaceful teachings, yes. But a religion cannot be judged only by its most conciliatory verses. It must also be judged by its authoritative texts, legal doctrines, and the way those doctrines have been interpreted by mainstream scholars over centuries. On that basis, Islam does not simply “promote peace”; it also contains clear religious mandates for armed struggle, coercive political domination, and unequal treatment of non-Muslims.

First, the Qur’an does not present war merely as an unfortunate last resort. It explicitly commands fighting in multiple passages. Qur’an 2:216 says: “Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you.” Qur’an 9:29 commands Muslims to “fight those who do not believe in Allah” among the People of the Book “until they give the jizya willingly while they are humbled.” Qur’an 8:39 similarly says to “fight them until there is no fitnah and the religion is entirely for Allah.” These are not pacifist texts; they are religious authorizations of warfare for theological and political ends.

Second, the hadith literature reinforces this. In both **Sahih al-Bukhari** and **Sahih Muslim**, among the most authoritative Sunni collections, Muhammad is reported to have said: “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah…” This statement has been enormously influential in Islamic jurisprudence. Likewise, **Sahih al-Bukhari 6922** records: “Whoever changes his religion, kill him,” a text historically used to support the death penalty for apostasy. A tradition that treats leaving the faith as a capital offense cannot straightforwardly be described as promoting peace in the modern sense of freedom of conscience.

Third, classical Islamic law developed a doctrine of **jihad** that was not limited to self-defense. Major scholars of Islamic legal history, including Majid Khadduri, Rudolph Peters, and David Cook, note that classical jurists often understood jihad as a collective duty of the Muslim community, including expansion of Muslim rule and subordination of non-Muslim populations through systems such as **dhimma** and **jizya**. This does not mean every Muslim endorsed violence, but it does mean that coercive warfare was not a fringe distortion; it was built into mainstream legal thought.

Fourth, Islamic history reflects this. Within a century of Muhammad’s death, Muslim armies had conquered vast territories across the Middle East, North Africa, Persia, and Spain. Like other empires, Muslim empires sometimes practiced tolerance and sometimes repression. But that history makes it impossible to claim that Islam’s political tradition is fundamentally one of peace. It was also a tradition of conquest, empire, and religiously justified rule.

The proposition may respond by quoting verses such as “There is no compulsion in religion” or “If they incline to peace, incline to it.” Those verses exist, and they matter. But they prove my point: Islamic sources are mixed. Islam contains calls to peace, but also commands to fight; protections for some non-Muslims, but also their legal subordination; spiritual teachings, but also political and military doctrines. Therefore, the fair conclusion is not that Islam simply “promotes peace,” but that Islam is a complex tradition containing both peaceful and coercive elements.

So the proposition fails because it asks us to accept a selective and sanitized version of the tradition. Many Muslims promote peace. Many Islamic interpretations promote peace. But Islam as a whole—judged by scripture, hadith, jurisprudence, and history—cannot honestly be said to promote peace in any simple or categorical sense.

### Citations

1. **Qur’an 2:216** — “Fighting has been prescribed for you…”  
2. **Qur’an 8:39** — “Fight them until there is no fitnah and the religion is entirely for Allah.”  
3. **Qur’an 9:29** — Command to fight People of the Book until they pay jizya.  
4. **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22** — “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify…”  
5. **Sahih al-Bukhari 6922** — “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
6. Majid Khadduri, *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, Johns Hopkins University Press, 1955.  
7. Rudolph Peters, *Jihad in Classical and Modern Islam*, Markus Wiener Publishers, 1996.  
8. David Cook, *Understanding Jihad*, University of California Press, 2005; 2nd ed. 2015.

round_1.for:
Chair, judges, and audience—

My opponent’s case rests on one central move: he equates **the existence of Islamic rules about war** with the claim that Islam does not promote peace. But that is a false standard. A tradition can promote peace while still permitting limited force against aggression, persecution, treachery, and public disorder. Modern international law does the same. The real question is not whether Islam is absolute pacifism; it is whether Islam’s normative direction is toward justice, restraint, reconciliation, protection of life, and peaceful coexistence. On that question, the answer remains yes.

## 1. Islam promotes peace, but it is not pacifism

My opponent quotes verses about fighting, such as Qur’an 2:216, 8:39, and 9:29. But none of these should be read in isolation from the Qur’an’s explicit limitations on warfare.

The governing principle is stated clearly:

> “Fight in the way of God those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, God does not love transgressors.”  
> **Qur’an 2:190**

This verse does two things: it permits fighting against aggressors, and it forbids transgression. That is not a blank cheque for violence; it is a doctrine of restraint.

The Qur’an also says:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also and trust in God.”  
> **Qur’an 8:61**

So even in wartime, peace is not rejected; it is commanded when the other side is willing.

And the first Qur’anic permission to fight was explicitly tied to persecution and expulsion:

> “Permission to fight is given to those who are fought, because they have been wronged… those who were expelled from their homes without right only because they said, ‘Our Lord is God.’”  
> **Qur’an 22:39–40**

Significantly, that passage says defensive struggle protects not only mosques, but also:

> “monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques.”  
> **Qur’an 22:40**

That is crucial. The Qur’an presents legitimate force as a means of resisting oppression and protecting religious freedom, not destroying it.

## 2. Qur’an 8:39 concerns persecution, not forced conversion

My opponent cites:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for God.”  
> **Qur’an 8:39**

But the word **fitnah** in this context refers to persecution, oppression, and the violent suppression of believers. The same idea appears in Qur’an 2:193:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah… but if they cease, then there is to be no aggression except against the oppressors.”  
> **Qur’an 2:193**

Notice the ending: **“if they cease,” hostilities cease.** That is not a command to fight until every person converts. It is a command to resist persecution until persecution stops.

This reading is reinforced by the Qur’an’s categorical rule:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

And:

> “The truth is from your Lord, so whoever wills, let him believe; and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.”  
> **Qur’an 18:29**

Therefore, verses about fighting cannot honestly be interpreted as general forced conversion without contradicting the Qur’an’s own explicit statements on freedom of conscience.

## 3. Qur’an 9:29 and jizya do not prove Islam promotes violence

My opponent also cites Qur’an 9:29 regarding fighting certain People of the Book until they pay **jizya**. But again, context matters. Sūrah 9 deals with conflict, treaty violations, and hostile forces. The same chapter commands Muslims to honour treaties with non-Muslims who have not betrayed them:

> “So long as they are upright toward you, be upright toward them.”  
> **Qur’an 9:7**

It also commands protection for a non-Muslim who seeks asylum:

> “If any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection so that he may hear the word of God, then deliver him to his place of safety.”  
> **Qur’an 9:6**

So even in one of the Qur’an’s sternest chapters, there are rules of treaty loyalty, asylum, and safe passage.

As for **jizya**, it was historically a tax on protected non-Muslim communities in exchange for security and exemption from military service. One may debate whether premodern systems meet modern ideals of equality, but it is inaccurate to portray jizya simply as “convert or die.” The Qur’an itself permits peaceful coexistence with non-Muslims:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you because of religion or expelled you from your homes. Indeed, God loves those who act justly.”  
> **Qur’an 60:8**

That verse is decisive: Islam does not command hostility toward peaceful non-Muslims. It commands **kindness and justice**.

## 4. The hadith “I was commanded to fight the people” must be read with the Qur’an and other hadith

My opponent cites the hadith:

> “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify that there is no god but Allah…”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 25; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 22**

But Islamic interpretation does not read one hadith in isolation. It is read alongside Qur’anic limits: no compulsion in religion, fight only those who fight you, accept peace, honour treaties, and protect non-combatants.

Classical commentators also recognized that “the people” in such reports may refer to a particular hostile group, not every human being on earth. The Prophet ﷺ made treaties with non-Muslims, accepted peaceful coexistence, and protected non-Muslim communities. If the hadith meant “fight every non-Muslim until conversion,” then the Prophet’s own treaties with Jews, Christians, and polytheists would make no sense.

The Prophet also said:

> “Whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3166**

And:

> “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 10; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 40**

These are not marginal narrations. They define Muslim conduct around safety, restraint, and protection of life.

## 5. Islamic law placed strict limits on warfare

My opponent argues that classical jihad doctrine was not always limited to self-defence. But even classical Islamic law developed substantial restrictions on war. The Prophet forbade killing non-combatants:

> Ibn ʿUmar reported that a woman was found killed in one of the battles, and the Prophet condemned the killing of women and children.  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3015; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1744**

He also instructed armies:

> “Do not act treacherously, do not mutilate, and do not kill children.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1731**

These rules are morally important. They show that even when war is permitted, Islam regulates it through limits: no treachery, no mutilation, no killing women and children, no transgression, and acceptance of peace.

That is much closer to a just-war ethic than a doctrine of aggression.

## 6. Apostasy texts are more complex than the opponent suggests

My opponent cites:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6922**

This is a serious text and should not be dismissed. But it must be interpreted within the wider Islamic source tradition.

First, the Qur’an mentions apostasy repeatedly but does not prescribe a worldly death penalty for mere private belief. For example:

> “Whoever among you turns back from his religion and dies while disbelieving, their deeds have become worthless…”  
> **Qur’an 2:217**

Also:

> “Those who believed, then disbelieved, then believed, then disbelieved, then increased in disbelief—God will not forgive them…”  
> **Qur’an 4:137**

This verse describes people changing belief more than once. If simple apostasy automatically required execution, the verse’s scenario would not make sense.

Second, another hadith describes the punishable case as one who:

> “leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> **Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6878; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 1676**

That wording matters. In the early Muslim community, apostasy was often tied to political treason, armed rebellion, or joining enemy forces. So many scholars, especially in modern Islamic legal thought, distinguish between private change of belief and public treason or violent rebellion.

Therefore, the apostasy issue cannot be used simplistically to claim Islam as a whole promotes violence. The Qur’anic baseline remains:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

## 7. History of conquest does not define the essence of Islam

My opponent points to early Muslim conquests. But historical empires are not the same thing as religious essence. Christianity has the Crusades, inquisitions, and colonial missions. Buddhism has had violent nationalist movements. Secular ideologies have produced world wars, gulags, and genocides. Yet we do not reduce those traditions to their worst political uses.

The fair method is to ask: what do the core teachings command?

Islam commands:

> “God commands justice, excellence, and giving to relatives, and forbids immorality, wrongdoing, and oppression.”  
> **Qur’an 16:90**

It commands reconciliation:

> “Reconciliation is best.”  
> **Qur’an 4:128**

It commands forgiveness and patience:

> “The servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth gently, and when the ignorant address them harshly, they say: peace.”  
> **Qur’an 25:63**

It commands mercy:

> “We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.”  
> **Qur’an 21:107**

And it commands justice even toward enemies:

> “Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just. Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.”  
> **Qur’an 5:8**

These are central, repeated moral principles.

## 8. The opponent’s conclusion is too strong

My opponent says Islam is “mixed.” But every serious moral tradition contains teachings about both peace and the use of force under certain conditions. The presence of rules for war does not mean a religion fails to promote peace. In fact, rules limiting war are themselves part of promoting peace.

Islam promotes peace by:

1. Prohibiting forced conversion — **Qur’an 2:256**  
2. Valuing human life — **Qur’an 5:32**  
3. Commanding justice even toward enemies — **Qur’an 5:8**  
4. Permitting kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims — **Qur’an 60:8**  
5. Limiting warfare to those who fight and forbidding transgression — **Qur’an 2:190**  
6. Requiring acceptance of peace when offered — **Qur’an 8:61**  
7. Protecting non-combatants — **Bukhārī 3015; Muslim 1744**  
8. Condemning the murder of protected non-Muslims — **Bukhārī 3166**

So the proposition does not require us to claim that every Muslim ruler was peaceful, or that every jurist reached modern liberal conclusions, or that Islam is absolute pacifism. It requires us to show that Islam’s moral and scriptural direction promotes peace, justice, restraint, mercy, and the protection of life.

On the evidence, that proposition stands. Islam does not promote chaos, aggression, or indiscriminate violence. It promotes peace with justice, peace with moral responsibility, and peace protected by restraint.
round_1.against:
Chair, judges, and audience—

My opponent’s reply is eloquent, but it depends on a repeated strategy: whenever Islamic texts command fighting, domination, or punishment, he narrows them to “context”; whenever Islamic texts speak of peace, he universalizes them. That is not a neutral method. The question is not whether Islam contains peaceful verses—it plainly does. The question is whether Islam, as a whole religious-legal system, can fairly be said to “promote peace.” The evidence still says no.

## 1. I am not demanding pacifism

My opponent says I falsely assume that promoting peace means absolute pacifism. I do not. A tradition may allow defensive force and still promote peace.

But Islam’s problem is not merely that it permits defensive war. The problem is that major Islamic sources and classical law authorize fighting for religious-political supremacy: conversion, tribute, or submission to Muslim rule. That goes beyond modern just-war self-defence.

A decisive hadith in **Sahih Muslim** records Muhammad instructing commanders:

> “When you meet your enemies who are polytheists, invite them to three things… Invite them to Islam… If they refuse, then ask them to pay jizya. If they refuse, then seek Allah’s help and fight them.”  
> **Sahih Muslim 1731a**

That is not merely “fight those who attack you.” It presents a religious ultimatum: Islam, tribute, or war. My opponent quotes the same hadith tradition for rules of restraint—“do not mutilate, do not kill children”—but he omits that the same report also authorizes coercive religious war.

Rules limiting violence do not automatically prove peace. Empires often regulate war. The question is whether the underlying system aims at peaceful equality or at enforced religious-political domination.

## 2. Qur’an 2:190 does not erase the later and broader fighting texts

My opponent treats Qur’an 2:190—“fight those who fight you, but do not transgress”—as the master rule. But the Qur’an also contains broader commands.

Immediately after 2:190, the text says:

> “Kill them wherever you find them…”  
> **Qur’an 2:191**

and:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah.”  
> **Qur’an 2:193**

Likewise:

> “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is entirely for Allah.”  
> **Qur’an 8:39**

My opponent says “fitnah” means only persecution. That is one possible reading, but not the only one historically. The phrase “until religion is for Allah” has often been read as a command to establish Islamic religious authority, not merely to stop attacks. The ambiguity itself damages the proposition. If a supposedly peace-promoting scripture contains commands that classical scholars could plausibly read as mandates for religious war, then the claim “Islam promotes peace” becomes too simplistic.

The same problem appears in Qur’an 9:29:

> “Fight those who do not believe in Allah… among the People of the Book until they pay the jizya by hand while they are humbled.”  
> **Qur’an 9:29**

This verse does not say, “Fight only those People of the Book who attack you.” It says to fight them until they pay jizya in a condition of subordination. My opponent calls jizya a tax in exchange for protection. But the verse’s own language—“while they are humbled” or “subdued”—shows that this is not peaceful coexistence among equals. It is peace through hierarchy.

## 3. “No compulsion in religion” does not solve the problem

My opponent repeatedly cites:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

But historically, Islamic law did not understand this to mean full religious liberty in the modern sense. It often meant that Jews and Christians were not necessarily forced to convert if they accepted Muslim rule and paid jizya. That is not the same as peace based on equal freedom of conscience.

A system can avoid forced conversion while still being coercive. “Convert, pay tribute in subordination, or face war” is not religious freedom. “Remain in your religion, but under inferior legal status” is not peaceful equality.

The same applies to apostasy. My opponent says apostasy laws are “complex.” They are. But complexity does not erase the fact that the most authoritative hadith collection states:

> “Whoever changes his religion, kill him.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6922**

Another report says lawful blood may include:

> “one who leaves his religion and separates from the community.”  
> **Sahih al-Bukhari 6878; Sahih Muslim 1676**

My opponent interprets that as treason. Some modern scholars do. But classical Islamic law generally did not limit the death penalty only to armed treason. Major jurists treated apostasy itself as a capital offence, usually after an opportunity to repent. Rudolph Peters and Gert de Vries summarize the classical position plainly: in traditional Islamic law, apostasy is punishable by death, with juristic disputes mainly over procedure and the treatment of women.  
See: Rudolph Peters and Gert J. J. de Vries, “Apostasy in Islam,” *Die Welt des Islams*, 1976.

So again, the problem is not a fringe extremist reading. The problem is that coercive doctrines existed in mainstream law.

## 4. Treaty protection and asylum do not negate coercive warfare

My opponent cites Qur’an 9:6, which grants protection to a polytheist seeking asylum, and Qur’an 9:7, which commands Muslims to honor treaties. Those verses exist. But they do not cancel Qur’an 9:29, Qur’an 9:5, or the hadith commanding commanders to offer Islam, jizya, or battle.

Qur’an 9:6 gives temporary safe conduct to someone seeking protection so that he may hear the message, then be delivered to safety. That is humane, but it does not prove a general doctrine of peaceful coexistence.

Similarly, treaty-keeping is not the same as a permanent commitment to religious peace. Many imperial systems honored treaties when useful while still maintaining an expansionist doctrine. Classical jihad law allowed truces, treaties, and protections, but that does not mean it rejected offensive expansion.

Majid Khadduri, in *War and Peace in the Law of Islam*, explains that classical Islamic jurisprudence treated jihad as a collective duty of the Muslim community and often understood peace with non-Muslim powers as temporary unless they entered Islamic rule or treaty arrangements. Rudolph Peters and David Cook make similar observations in their studies of jihad doctrine.

## 5. Non-combatant rules are morally important—but insufficient

My opponent cites hadiths forbidding the killing of women and children:

> **Sahih al-Bukhari 3015; Sahih Muslim 1744**

and commands against treachery and mutilation:

> **Sahih Muslim 1731**

I accept that these are real restraints. But restraints within war do not prove that the system promotes peace. A legal tradition may forbid killing children yet still authorize expansionary war against adult populations. That is not pacifism, and more importantly, it is not a clear promotion of peace.

Also, the same **Sahih Muslim 1731** that forbids treachery and killing children also tells commanders to invite enemies to Islam, then jizya, then war. My opponent cannot use half the hadith as proof of peace while ignoring the other half as evidence of coercion.

## 6. History matters because the conquests were not accidental

My opponent says history of empire does not define religious essence. True, but Islam’s early conquests were not distant distortions centuries later. They occurred immediately after Muhammad’s death under the Rashidun caliphs—the very generation closest to the Prophet. Muslim armies conquered Syria, Egypt, Persia, North Africa, and beyond, and later jurists developed doctrines explaining and legitimizing such expansion as jihad.

This matters because the proposition is not “some Muslims promote peace.” It is “Islam promotes peace.” If the earliest Muslim political community and the classical juristic tradition both included religiously justified conquest, then conquest cannot simply be dismissed as an abuse unrelated to Islam.

## 7. The opponent proves my original point: Islam is mixed

My opponent lists peaceful teachings: mercy, justice, reconciliation, kindness to peaceful non-Muslims. I acknowledge those teachings. But they do not erase the other side of the record:

- Fighting is “prescribed” for believers — **Qur’an 2:216**  
- Fighting continues until religion is for Allah — **Qur’an 8:39; 2:193**  
- People of the Book may be fought until they pay jizya in subordination — **Qur’an 9:29**  
- Commanders are instructed to offer Islam, jizya, or battle — **Sahih Muslim 1731a**  
- Muhammad is reported to have said he was commanded to fight people until they testify to Islam — **Sahih al-Bukhari 25; Sahih Muslim 22**  
- Apostasy is punished by death in authoritative hadith and classical law — **Sahih al-Bukhari 6922**

So the fair conclusion is not that Islam is only violent. That would be false and unfair. But it is equally false to claim that Islam simply “promotes peace.” The tradition contains peace, but also coercive warfare, legal inequality, religious supremacy, and punishment for leaving the faith.

Therefore, the proposition fails. Many Muslims promote peace. Many Islamic interpretations promote peace. But Islam as a scriptural, legal, and historical system cannot honestly be reduced to “a religion of peace.” It is a mixed tradition, and the coercive elements are too authoritative and too central to ignore.

conclusions.for:
Chair, honourable judges, respected opponents, and audience—

In conclusion, the proposition before us is not that every Muslim ruler in history was peaceful, nor that Islam is absolute pacifism, nor that no difficult texts exist in Islamic tradition. The proposition is that **Islam promotes peace**. And throughout this debate, we have shown that this claim is firmly supported by Islam’s core teachings.

Islam promotes peace first through its foundational values. Its greeting is peace. Its moral language is rooted in mercy, justice, safety, and submission to God. The Qur’an commands:

> “There is no compulsion in religion.”  
> **Qur’an 2:256**

It declares the sanctity of human life:

> “Whoever kills a soul… it is as if he had slain mankind entirely; and whoever saves one, it is as if he had saved mankind entirely.”  
> **Qur’an 5:32**

It commands justice even toward enemies:

> “Do not let hatred of a people prevent you from being just.”  
> **Qur’an 5:8**

And it permits kindness and justice toward peaceful non-Muslims:

> “God does not forbid you from being kind and just toward those who have not fought you…”  
> **Qur’an 60:8**

These are not isolated or marginal ideas. They are central ethical principles.

My opponent has argued that because Islam contains rules about fighting, Islam cannot be said to promote peace. But that standard is mistaken. A tradition can promote peace while still allowing limited force in cases of aggression, persecution, and oppression. Modern law does the same. The question is whether force is unlimited or restrained. In Islam, it is restrained.

The Qur’an says:

> “Fight those who fight you, but do not transgress.”  
> **Qur’an 2:190**

And:

> “If they incline to peace, then incline to it also.”  
> **Qur’an 8:61**

That is not a doctrine of aggression. It is a doctrine of moral restraint: do not initiate injustice, do not transgress, and accept peace when peace is possible.

We also showed that verses about fighting must be read in context. The first permission to fight was given to people who had been persecuted and expelled from their homes, and the Qur’an even says such resistance protects monasteries, churches, synagogues, and mosques. That is not religious tyranny; it is protection against oppression.

The Prophet Muhammad’s teachings reinforce this peaceful ethic. He said:

> “The Muslim is the one from whose tongue and hand people are safe.”

He condemned the killing of women and children. He prohibited treachery and mutilation. He warned that whoever kills a person under covenant will not smell the fragrance of Paradise. These teachings establish safety, restraint, and protection of life as marks of true Islamic conduct.

My opponent also relied on history—conquests, empires, and political conflicts. But no religion should be judged only by the actions of states and rulers. Christianity is not reduced to the Crusades. Democracy is not reduced to every war fought by democratic countries. Likewise, Islam should be judged by its core principles, not by every political abuse committed in its name.

The fair conclusion is this: Islam is not a pacifist tradition, but it is a peace-promoting tradition. It promotes peace through justice, mercy, freedom of conscience, protection of innocent life, treaty loyalty, limits on warfare, and reconciliation.

So when Islam is read responsibly—through its Qur’anic principles, prophetic teachings, and moral objectives—it does not promote chaos, hatred, or indiscriminate violence. It promotes peace with justice, peace with dignity, and peace grounded in accountability before God.

For these reasons, I proudly affirm the proposition:

**Islam promotes peace.**
conclusions.against:
Chair, judges, and audience—

Let me close by making clear what my argument has **not** been. I have not argued that Muslims are inherently violent. I have not argued that Islam contains no teachings of mercy, restraint, justice, or reconciliation. It plainly does. Many Muslims live peaceful lives and sincerely understand their faith as a source of peace.

But that is not the proposition before us. The proposition is that **Islam promotes peace**. That is a broad claim about Islam as a scriptural, legal, and historical tradition. And my case has been that this claim is too selective and too simple.

Throughout this debate, I have shown that Islamic sources contain not only peaceful exhortations, but also authoritative commands and doctrines involving coercion and religious-political domination.

The Qur’an says:

- “Fighting has been prescribed for you” — **Qur’an 2:216**
- “Fight them until there is no fitnah and religion is for Allah” — **Qur’an 2:193; 8:39**
- “Fight those who do not believe…” among the People of the Book until they pay **jizya** while humbled — **Qur’an 9:29**

The hadith literature reinforces this problem. In the most authoritative Sunni collections, Muhammad is reported to have said:

- “I have been commanded to fight the people until they testify…” — **Bukhari 25; Muslim 22**
- “Whoever changes his religion, kill him” — **Bukhari 6922**

And in **Sahih Muslim 1731**, commanders are instructed to invite enemies to Islam, then jizya, and if they refuse, to fight. That is not merely a defensive rule against aggression. It is a religious ultimatum: conversion, submission, or war.

My opponent has repeatedly appealed to peaceful verses: “no compulsion in religion,” “if they incline to peace, incline to it,” “do not transgress,” and so on. I accept that those verses exist. But they do not erase the other texts. They prove my point: Islam is not simply a peace tradition; it is a mixed tradition.

Nor can the problem be solved by saying these fighting texts are all contextual. Context matters, yes. But for centuries, major classical jurists did not reduce jihad to modern self-defence. They developed doctrines of expansion, dhimma, jizya, apostasy punishment, and the subordination of non-Muslims under Islamic rule. These were not fringe extremist inventions. They were part of mainstream Islamic legal history.

History confirms the same pattern. The earliest Muslim community did not merely preach private spirituality. Within a century of Muhammad’s death, Muslim armies had conquered vast territories. Like other empires, Islamic empires sometimes showed tolerance and sometimes showed repression. But conquest and religiously justified rule were undeniably part of the tradition.

So the central issue is this: a religion that contains peaceful teachings may still fail to “promote peace” in any categorical sense if it also contains authoritative doctrines of coercive warfare, unequal legal status, and punishment for apostasy.

That is why the proposition fails.

The fair conclusion is not “Islam is only violent.” That would be false. The fair conclusion is also not “Islam simply promotes peace.” That is equally false. The honest conclusion is that Islam contains both peaceful and coercive elements, and the coercive elements are too scriptural, too legal, and too historical to be dismissed.

Many Muslims promote peace. Many Islamic interpretations promote peace. But Islam as a whole—judged by its scriptures, hadith, jurisprudence, and early history—cannot honestly be reduced to the claim that it promotes peace.

For that reason, I urge you to reject the proposition.
